newsitem.title: USA: Monsanto sees more gene-altered crops in 97.
newsitem.headline: Monsanto sees more gene-altered crops in 97.

text.p: Protests over the use of genetically altered crops have had little impact on consumer confidence, and should not stop growth in acreage devoted to herbicide-resistant soybeans or pest-resistant corn, an official with drug giant Monsanto Co said Sunday.

"There could be as much as 10 percent of next year's corn crop in Bt production," Dr. Molly Cline, director of food industry relations for St. Louis, Mo.-based Monsanto, told a meeting of grain elevator operators sponsored by the National Grain and Feed Association.
Monsanto already produces herbicide-resistant Roundup Ready soybeans, and will have corn that includes the Bt protein, resistant to the European corn borer, available to producers this year.

Final yield data from the 1996-97 U.S. soybean crop will be needed to more accurately forecast the number of acres planted with Monsanto's Roundup Ready soybeans during the 1997-98, but the company has put early acreage estimates at 5 to 10 million acres, Cline said.

Citing a Monsanto-sponsored survey of 1,058 farmers who planted the genetically altered soybeans in 1996, Cline said 53 percent said they would plant again next year, while 32 percent said they would probably plant Roundup Ready soybeans again. Many were waiting for final yield data before making 1997 planting decisions, she said.

Yield results were still being gathered, but Cline said final data was expected soon as the U.S. crop has been harvested. There has been some talk in U.S. cash grain markets that producers were disappointed with initial yields.
The use of Roundup Ready soybeans has drawn worldwide protests from environmentalists and critics who say that genetically altered crops have no place in the food chain.
However, most regulatory bodies in Europe, Japan and the U.S. have determined that the crops are safe for feed and food usage. The European Union has not yet given approval for the use of Bt corn.
"Acceptance will vary by country, but for most consumers there are bigger (food safety) issues," Cline said.
According to a survey sponsored by the U.S. trade group the Food Marketing Institute, consumers in the U.S. said spoilage and pesticide residues are the top food safety concerns.
Roundup Ready soybeans that have already been harvested and sold in the U.S. and the beans "have moved into the grain trade business as usual despite some background noise, " Cline told the group.
The Roundup Ready soybeans are commercially available and have been approved for usage in Canada and Argentina, and are being tested in Brazil, Cline said.
